bib.title: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents

SOURCE: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents. Shunyu Yao, Howard Chen (equal contribution), John Yang, Karthik Narasimhan (Princeton). NeurIPS 2022, arXiv 2207.01206v4 (8 Feb 2023).
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/yao-2022-webshop.pdf

COVERAGE: 28 of 28 pages, 86,230 of 86,230 chars. That covers the main text, NeurIPS checklist, Appendices A–E (reward calculation, reward verification, model details, ablations, sim-to-real, limitations) and the human-trajectory instruction document (pp. 23–28). I skimmed the references for origins only.

CLAIMS
- claim: The two metrics are different things. Task Score is the average partial-credit reward. Success Rate counts only episodes with full reward, and full reward does not require buying the exact target product.
  number: Score = 100 × avg reward; SR = share with r = 1
  setup: all WebShop evaluations
  quote: "(1)Task Score: deﬁned as (100×avg. reward), which captures the average reward obtained across episodes; and (2) Success Rate (SR) deﬁned as the portion of instructions wherer = 1. Note that it is possible to obtain r = 1 for an episode even if the ﬁnal product is noty∗"
  where: p.5
- claim: Reward is computed programmatically from the final purchased state. It is the fraction of the instruction's attributes, options and price constraint that the bought product satisfies, multiplied by a type-match factor. The extraction garbles the fraction layout. Read from the paper's own sub-score definitions on p.8, it is r = r_type · (|U_att∩Y_att| + |U_opt∩Y_opt| + 1[y_price ≤ u_price]) / (|U_att| + |U_opt| + 1).
  number: r ∈ [0,1]
  setup: a reward is given once, at the end, when choose[buy] is taken. Attributes are hidden from the agent.
  quote: "r =rtype·|Uatt∩Yatt| +|Uopt∩Yopt| + 1[yprice≤uprice]|Uatt| +|Uopt| + 1 (1)"; sub-scores "1) attribute score (|Uatt∩Yatt|/|Uatt|), 2) option score (|Uopt∩Yopt|/|Uopt|), 3) price score (1[yprice≤uprice]), and 4) type score (rtype)"
  where: p.5 (Eq. 1), p.8
- claim: r_type is a step function of a noun-only title string match, combined with coarse- and fine-grained category match. Its purpose is to stop a reward for "obviously different types of products" (e.g. butter vs plant-based meat) that share attributes.
  number: 0 / 0.1 / 0.5 / 1
  setup: TextMatch uses SpaCy NOUN/PROPN tokens of titles
  quote: "rtype = 0, if TextMatch(¯y, ¯y∗) = 0 / 0.1, if TextMatch(¯y, ¯y∗)< 0.1 / 0.5, if TextMatch(¯y, ¯y∗)> 0.2 andc = 1 andf = 1, / 1, otherwise (6)" (line breaks flattened)
  where: p.17
- claim: Headline results. The best model reaches about 29% success, the rule baseline 9.6%, human experts 59%.
  number: 29% / 9.6% / 59%
  setup: 500 test instructions; models in simple mode, humans in HTML mode
  quote: "Our best model achieves a task success rate of 29%, which outperforms rule-based heuristics (9.6%) but is far lower than human expert performance (59%)."
  where: p.1
- claim: Full table on the test split, averaged over 3 trials. Rule scores 45.6 / 9.6%, IL 59.9 / 29.1%, IL+RL 62.4 / 28.7%, human expert 82.1 / 59.6%. RL fine-tuning raises the score but slightly lowers success, so the two metrics rank the models differently.

LIMITS
- The reward uses exact matching, so it systematically under-scores: "a consistent tendency to over-penalize the picked product ... This under-scoring is a result of our reward function's exact matching criterion" (p.19). Synonyms such as lightweight vs easy carry get no credit.
- An r = 1 can be reached with a product that is not y* (p.5). Success means the product meets the spec, not that it is the target item.
- The reward checks only the final purchased state. Trajectory quality, efficiency and cost are not scored.
- Attributes are TF-IDF bigrams filtered by hand, so they can be generic ("easy to use"). Options can be very specific, and agents may use an option as a shortcut while ignoring the rest of the instruction (p.22). Attribute labelling may carry labeller bias.
- The reward and instructions are text-only. Images barely matter (IL without images 60.3/28.4 vs 60.6/29.0, Table 10, p.20). Reviews are not used.
- The split is i.i.d. with no category-level generalisation split. The data is US/English Amazon only.
- Sim-to-real uses 100 instructions with manual scoring. Buy and option actions were held in the interface rather than executed on the real site (p.22). The paper has internal inconsistencies: human Amazon score is 88.2 in Table 5 but "88.0" in the text; rule SR is 9.6% vs "10%"; IL+RL length is 4.5 vs "4.8".
- Dated: these are pre-LLM-agent models (BERT/BART IL+RL). Later prompted-LLM agents are not covered.
- The human expert gap is partly crowd-worker impatience, which the authors concede (footnote p.3, Table 7 p.18).

BUILDS ON: World of Bits / MiniWoB (Shi et al., 2017); WikiNav (Nogueira and Cho, 2016); WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021), contrasted because it needs human-in-the-loop evaluation; workflow-guided exploration (Liu et al., 2018); Klarna product page dataset (Hotti et al., 2021); BERT (Devlin et al., 2019); BART (Lewis et al., 2019); ResNet (He et al., 2016); A3C-style policy gradient (Mnih et al., 2016); BiDAF cross-attention (Seo et al., 2016); CALM text-game action generation (Yao et al., 2020); language drift (Lazaridou et al., 2020); Pyserini BM25 (Lin et al., 2021); OpenAI Gym (Brockman et al., 2016).

CODE: none. The project site is https://webshop-pnlp.github.io (p.1).

FIGURES
- Figure 1, p.2: "The WebShop environment. A: An example task trajectory in HTML mode ... (5) ﬁnally buy the product to end the episode and receive a rewardr∈ [0, 1] (§3.2). B: the results page in simple mode ... C: The product notation used in §3 ... The attributesYatt are hidden from the task performer." This is the best candidate. One picture shows a trajectory ending in a purchased state, with the hidden attributes, options and price that the reward is computed against, so it makes "grade the outcome by state" concrete.
- Alternative: Table 2, p.8 (score breakdown by attribute, option, type and price). It shows in one glance why partial credit and success diverge.

PROBLEMS: Eq. 1 and Eq. 6 lose their fraction and case layout in extraction. I reconstructed the formula above from the p.8 sub-score definitions and flagged it as a reconstruction. LaTeX base64 blobs appear on pp.2 and 6. The Figure 4 bar values are flattened ("45.645.8 59.9 56.0 52.5 55.2 62.4 / 9.610.6 29.126.3 11.2 17.6 28.7"), so I quoted ablation bars only where the text states them. Appendix C.2 contains a stray duplicated paragraph about the Choice oracle. The appendix human-instruction document includes advice addressed to MTurk workers, which is task material and not addressed to me. No embedded instructions aimed at an AI reader were found.
